Right now, users are required to initialize the entire model using the same seed among ranks before wrapping the model as FSDP instance. This impacts usability and also initialization performance.
Once #64394 new API is done, FSDP initialization can be done inside FSDP constructor and can be done on the device directly.
There are a few approaches to improve FSDP initialization.

Rank0 initializes the layers, and then scatter the shards to other ranks. In this way, the same seed is not required, but it requires scatter communication
Every rank only initializes its own shard once the shard is materialized, this requires module to support initializing partial tensor of a parameter, also the same seed is required
Every rank initializes some layers in parallel, and then scatter shards to other layers. In this way, the same seed is not required, it also requires scatter communication, but initialization is parallelized and performance could be improved as well

Right now, FSDP assumes each rank has the same number of gradients to be updated and these gradients are updated in the same order among ranks.
It maintains one fixed bucket, once a grad is updated, the grad is put into the bucket, once the bucket is full, it starts to kick off synchronization communication.
There are a few cases could break the assumptions and cause inaccurate results or hangs:

each rank trains different subgraphs of a model
grad ready order may not always be the same among ranks for some applications

We need to add a check to make sure updated gradients are the same and these gradients are updated in the same order among ranks, otherwise throw errors; Or redesign the syntonization approach to support cases when each rank trains different subgraphs of a model or grad ready order is not he same among ranks.

nodes.bodyText:
Usually checkpoint a model happens on root FSDP instance, there are two ways to checkpoint a model usually:

call state_dict() to checkpoint/save full original params in rank 0 if models can fit into one rank's memory, it is slow as it requires to all gather shards before checkpointing; then call load_state_dict() to load full original params into each rank, and shard it
call local_state_dict() to checkpoint/save local shard in each rank in parallel, right now it checkpoints a flat_parameter with local shard data;  then call load_local_state_dict() to load the local shard into each rank

once #64464 is done, the local_state_dict() will checkpoint original parameters with local shard data of a flat tensor, each parameter could be pointed to a full tensor or partial tensor or empty;  we need to add unit tests to make sure this works as expected once #64464 is done.
Reshard checkpoint APIs
In distributed inference or fine tuning cases, the world size may change, the local state dicts can not be simply loaded by calling load_local_state_dict().
We need to provide APIs to merge shards into original full params:

if these original full params can fit into memory, each rank can create a original model and load these original full params, then wrap the model as FSDP instances to shard layers
if these original full params can not fit into memory, each rank possibly needs to create a original model on meta device, we need an API to load these full params layer by layer while materializing these layers, and then shard these layers

🚀 Feature
We have pass in JIT execution which attempts to batch matrix multiplication in order to improve performance. It was written before JIT IR supported mutability, and so currently it bails for any block with a mutable operator. A write to a dictionary obviously  does not invalidate matrix multiplication batching. We can improve our handling here by just checking that none of the inputs to a matrix multiplication are written to with the Alias Db hasWriters API. We probably want to lazily initialize the aliasdb when we first see aten::mm because not all models have matrix multiplications in them.
Testing: this was added a long time ago and we test a little bit more now lol but I would recommend writing functions in python, binding the pass, and then invoking it and see if mutation is correctly handled on the resulting IR. Test peephole has examples of similar tests.

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 Feature
Provide an option for "reusing" tensors passed into load_state_dict() as module parameters. This would help reduce memory usage when loading a module from a state_dict.
Motivation
Currently, loading a model in the canonical way requires 2x the memory of the parameters: one set of parameters within the model and one set of parameters within the state_dict. This can be a problem for models that are too large for two copies to fit within memory. Example:
import torch

# Loads one set of parameters into memory.
m = MyModule()

# Loads a second set of parameters into memory.
state_dict = torch.load('foo.pt')

m.load_state_dict(state_dict)
There should be an officially-supported way to load a module with only one set of parameters in memory at once.
Pitch
One way to avoid the extra copy of the parameters is to instantiate the module with device='meta' so as not to allocate any storage.
import torch

m = MyModule(device='meta')
state_dict = torch.load('foo.pt')
m.load_state_dict(state_dict)

# Problem: module parameters are still meta tensors; loading didn't work.
However, this currently doesn't work because load_state_dict() copies data into  the module parameters when loading; the module's parameters will still be on the meta device after the call to load_state_dict().
One way to address this is to implement a flag that "reuses" the state_dict tensors passed in to load_state_dict(). With this set, the underlying data for module parameters will be swapped out to reference the same memory as the state_dict tensors. Note that this would also require set_data() to be implemented for meta tensors, allowing them to be converted to non-meta tensors.
Thus, only one copy of the module parameters needs to exist in memory for the module to be loaded. Also, since the parameters remain the same objects, optimizers that reference them will still work.
import torch

m = MyModule(device='meta')
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(m.parameters(), lr=0.01)

state_dict = torch.load('foo.pt')
m.load_state_dict(state_dict, reuse_tensors=True)

# Module parameters now reference the same data as state_dict tensors.
# The optimizer defined above will still correctly operate on the
# module's parameters.
Alternatives

Implement incremental module loading to avoid needing two full copies of the parameter sets in memory at once (#64327).
Do nothing and continue to require users to write their own loading logic to sidestep this issue.

cc @VitalyFedyunin @ngimel @heitorschueroff @albanD @mruberry @jbschlosser @walterddr

🚀 Feature
Forward mode automatic differentiation (Forward AD) is useful for computing Jacobian-vector-products of mappings 𝕂ⁿ → 𝕂ᵐ, especially when m>>n.
Forward AD was recently added to PyTorch and we need more rules coverage. The process of adding a forward AD rule is similar to the one for adding reverse AD rules.
When implementing a new rule always start with tools/autograd/derivatives.yaml, this is the file where all autograd rules are registered.
Let's look at the rule for linalg_inv_ex:
- name: linalg_inv_ex(Tensor self, *, bool check_errors=False) -> (Tensor inverse, Tensor info)
  self: -at::matmul(inverse.conj().transpose(-2, -1), at::matmul(grad, inverse.conj().transpose(-2, -1)))
  inverse: -at::matmul(at::matmul(inverse, self_t), inverse)

Let A=self and C=inverse, then the reverse AD rule is "A̅ = −Cᴴ C̅ Cᴴ" and the forward AD rule is "Ċ = −C Ȧ C".
In the above schema self: includes the code to compute A̅ and inverse: has the code for computing Ċ.
The tangents of input variables have the suffix _t in the code.
If the code for the derivative rule is too complex to fit in one line of derivatives.yaml file,
then a C++ function can be added to torch/csrc/autograd/FunctionsManual.h implementing the rule in torch/csrc/autograd/FunctionsManual.cpp.
Tests of the forward AD support of a specific function can be enabled with supports_forward_ad=True in OpInfo of the corresponding operator in torch/testing/_internal/common_methods_invocations.py.
Some useful resources for rules and derivations:


M. Giles "An extended collection of matrix derivative results for forward and reverse mode automatic differentiation"
https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:8d0c0a29-c92b-4153-a1d2-38b276e93124

Thanks Min Xu's initial idea and discussion about redesign FSDP flatten parameter.
Right now all the original parameters of a module are cat into a big flat tensor, this flat tensor is registered as a new parameter of the module, and it is called "flat_parameter". All the original parameters of the module are de-registered and are set as general attributes of the module.  After flattening, the big flat tensor is sharded into chunks, each rank keeps one chunk of the tensor.
In this way, all_gather() this big flat tensor from other ranks could only be called once during forward, and thus it is efficient.
However, this also caused usability issue because of this newly introduced parameter and de-registered original parameters.  Usually users expect original parameter names to be kept and they may have some processing outside of FSDP that is based on these original parameter names (e.g. checkpoint file and optimizer states expect original parameters usually).
So we may need to redesign this flatten parameter method. Solutions could be:

Instead of registering the new 'flat_parameter', allocate buffers to hold the flat tensor that cats tensors of original parameters, original parameters will be kept and be views of the flat tensor. This is similar to the "gradient_as_bucket_view" feature in DDP
not flatten tensor in advance, instead of all_gather a flat tensor once, we can introduce a new collective call 'all_gather_coaleced' that can all gather a list of parameters tensors once, this may need to copy the list of parameter tensors to a buffer every time when 'all_gather_coaleced' is called and introduce some performance regression. but this approach could simplify FSDP implementation

Python 3.10 RC 1 is available. Python release policy has changed, and RC 1 is now the point where the ABI is frozen. There are a decent number of users who, intentionally or not, install Python 3.10.0 right after it is released. At which point they find that they need binaries. As a result, the Python core team is encouraging project to already upload wheels to PyPI.
For more context, see numpy/numpy#19630 (comment).
Pitch

 Add Python 3.10 in CI
 Add Python 3.10 support in the builder repo for wheels and conda packages
 Upload wheels to PyPI and conda packages to the pytorch channel with the next minor or bugfix release

Alternatives
Just wait and add 3.10 support later.
Additional context
It seems unlikely that there will be changes between RC 1 and final that would affect PyTorch binaries (as unlikely as between 3.10.x and 3.10.x+1). Operators interact with systems like autograd that require separate tests
Tests like this can be tricky to write because there is no readily available reference and specifying the golden values is cumbersome for anything but small tensors
The results of an operation differ platform to platform
It's important to test that the output has additional properties

But it's still a common and extremely useful class of test.
Recently OpInfos were extended to support references and automatic reference testing of their sample inputs against them, but an OpInfos sample inputs are typically small, both in number and the size of the tensors they use. This is because sample inputs are reused by a wide variety of tests and PyTorch is very sensitive to test time. This does create a natural question, however: "why do specify a larger set of reference inputs in a separate test and then a subset of them as sample inputs on an OpInfo?" It seems like these could be combined into one.
One simple way to do this would be to extend OpInfos' sample inputs functions to take a new kwarg that would return the bigger set of reference inputs, but there are other possible solutions.

🐛 Bug
I have a model with multiple outputs. Sometimes, certain outputs are missing, so they are NaN, and when calculating the loss they should be ignored. This can be done in two ways:

Mask out the missing outputs, then calculate the loss on the rest
Calculate the loss for each output (giving NaN for missing outputs) then mask out the NaNs

These should be equivalent, but they are not. The second can lead to NaNs in the gradient. See the example below.
To Reproduce
import torch

torch.manual_seed(0)

m = torch.nn.Linear(1, 2, bias = False)

x = torch.tensor([[0.0]])
y = torch.tensor([[float('nan'), 0.0]])
y_mask = ~torch.isnan(y)
y_pred = m(x)

def loss_fn(y_pred, y):
	# problem shows up when using l2 or log loss (but not l1)
	return torch.square(y_pred - y)

# these two branches should be equivalent; they aren't
if True: # (1) mask after loss_fn

else:    # (2) mask before loss_fn
	l = loss_fn(y_pred[y_mask], y[y_mask])

# loss is fine: no NaNs
print("loss:", l)
assert not torch.any(torch.isnan(l))

l.sum().backward()

# grad should not have NaNs
assert not torch.any(torch.isnan(m.weight.grad))

🚀 Feature
There is currently no effective way to convert between Pytorch and OrtValue and vice versa without using NumPy. There should be a way to create a Pytorch tensor from the data pointer in GPU memory, shape, and type, which can be provided by OrtValue.
Motivation
I'm trying to convert a seq2seq model from Pytorch to Onnx. The beam search implementation includes lots of operations in Pytorch, so the outputs of the encoder and the previous step of the decoder have to be converted from OrtValue to Pytorch tensor, then back to OrtValue. I have found no direct conversion method except for using Numpy as the medium, i.e. converting Pytorch/OrtValue to Numpy then to OrtValue/Pytorch, which causes CPU-GPU data copying overhead. Since the memory allocation can be derived from OrtValue via start pointer, shape, and data type, we should have a way to create Pytorch tensors from these values.
Additional context
Here is my conversion code via NumPy as a reference.
input_ids_np = input_ids.cpu().numpy()
attention_mask_np = attention_mask.cpu().numpy()
input_ids_ortvalue = onnxruntime.OrtValue.ortvalue_from_numpy(input_ids_np, 'cuda', 0)
attention_mask_ortvalue = onnxruntime.OrtValue.ortvalue_from_numpy(attention_mask_np, 'cuda', 0)
io_binding = self.encoder.io_binding()
io_binding.bind_input(name='input_ids', device_type=input_ids_ortvalue.device_name(), device_id=0,
                      element_type=np.longlong, shape=input_ids_ortvalue.shape(),
                      buffer_ptr=input_ids_ortvalue.data_ptr())
io_binding.bind_input(name='attention_mask', device_type=attention_mask_ortvalue.device_name(), device_id=0,
                      element_type=np.longlong, shape=attention_mask_ortvalue.shape(),
                      buffer_ptr=attention_mask_ortvalue.data_ptr())
io_binding.bind_output('hidden_states', 'cuda')
self.encoder.run_with_iobinding(io_binding)
# The following call returns an OrtValue which has data allocated by ONNX Runtime on CUDA
encoder_hidden_state = io_binding.get_outputs()[0]
return BaseModelOutput(torch.tensor(encoder_hidden_state.numpy(), dtype=torch.float32).to(self.device))

🚀 Feature
SVD on GPU for a large matrix (usually with size > 1024) or an ill-conditioned matrix may throw runtime error because of not converging well.
SVD on GPU currently uses the iterative Jacobi method of cusolverDn<T>gesvdj (note the trailing j). The pytorch implementation takes cusolver default values of max sweeps = 100 and tolerance = machine accuracy. The cusolver gesvdj engine stops when either the accuracy or max sweeps is achieved. From the cusolver doc, usually ~15 sweeps would be enough.
The gesvdj method works well and is much faster than the QR-based method of cusolverDn<T>gesvd for small size matrix (benchmark #48436 (comment)). However, for large size matrix, we've received several reports with runtime errors because SVD is not converged well, e.g. #28293 (comment)
To fix this issue, there are several approaches


Expose the max sweeps and tolerance of cusolver gesvdj to user, so that people can set them to stricter values as needed.
Problem: what should the user interface look like? Extra kwargs for torch.linalg.svd? Note that the CPU LAPACK method doesn't have this issue and won't use those parameters.


Add gesvd method to pytorch.
Problem: what should the user interface look like? The entrance of SVD is only torch.linalg.svd and how should user change the backend engine? Extra kwargs or extra python functions?


Add gesvd method to pytorch, and use gesvd as a fallback when gesvdj doesn't converge.
Problem: this would make SVD performance much worse in those cases.


Note that the QR-based gesvd method always converges. This issue doesn't affect the batched gesvdjBatched method which only takes matrices with size <= 32 and converges well in nearly all cases.

Currently we have the following concepts in our CI scripts/test structure:


The idea of a job prefix, used when trying to consolidate test time stats between build and test jobs. Relevant code 
  
    
      pytorch/tools/testing/test_selections.py
    
    
        Lines 25 to 35
      in
      f2c47cf
    
  
  
    

        
          
           def _get_stripped_CI_job() -> str: 
        

        
          
               """E.g. convert 'pytorch_windows_vs2019_py36_cuda10.1_build' to 'pytorch_windows_vs2019_py36_cuda10.1'. 
        

        
          
               """ 
        

        
          
               job = os.environ.get("JOB_BASE_NAME", "").rstrip('0123456789') 
        

        
          
               if job.endswith('_slow_test'): 
        

        
          
                   job = job[:len(job) - len('_slow_test')] 
        

        
          
               elif job.endswith('_test') or job.endswith('-test'): 
        

        
          
                   job = job[:len(job) - len('_test')] 
        

        
          
               elif job.endswith('_build') or job.endswith('-build'): 
        

        
          
                   job = job[:len(job) - len('_build')] 
        

        
          
               return job 
        
    
  




The idea of a job name, which is the most specific one could go with test names, used here 
  
    
      pytorch/tools/stats/print_test_stats.py
    
    
        Lines 782 to 793
      in
      f2c47cf
    
  
  
    

        
          
           def send_report_to_s3(head_report: Version2Report) -> None: 
        

        
          
               job = os.getenv('JOB_BASE_NAME', os.environ.get('CIRCLE_JOB')) 
        

        
          
               # SHARD_NUMBER is specific to GHA jobs, as the shard number would be included in CIRCLE_JOB already 
        

        
          
               shard = os.environ.get('SHARD_NUMBER', '') 
        

        
          
               sha1 = os.environ.get('CIRCLE_SHA1') 
        

        
          
               branch = os.environ.get('CIRCLE_BRANCH', '') 
        

        
          
               now = datetime.datetime.utcnow().isoformat() 
        

        
          
               if branch not in ['master', 'nightly'] and not branch.startswith("release/"): 
        

        
          
                   pr = os.environ.get('CIRCLE_PR_NUMBER', 'unknown') 
        

        
          
                   key = f'pr_test_time/{pr}/{sha1}/{job}{shard}/{now}Z.json.bz2'  # Z meaning UTC 
        

        
          
               else: 
        

        
          
                   key = f'test_time/{sha1}/{job}{shard}/{now}Z.json.bz2'  # Z meaning UTC 
        
    
  




The idea of a build environment, which is used everywhere in our build and test scripts in .jenkins/pytorch.


To address those concepts, we use the following environment variables:

BUILD_ENVIRONMENT: this is sometimes used as ALL three of the concepts above
JOB_BASE_NAME: this attempts to be a job name but is not very specific on GHA and is specific on Circle because we set JOB_BASE_NAME to CIRCLE_JOB. This variable is also used to derive BUILD_ENVIRONMENT like the first code example above.

All this is not fun to deal with. We should clean it up. A good idea is to revamp what we mean by BUILD_ENVIRONMENT and JOB_BASE_NAME.
Example proposal:

BUILD_ENVIRONMENT: should represent the environment in which pytorch was built! This could also function as a great job prefix.
JOB_NAME: should represent the most specific description of a job. This would include test config and shard number and all that good stuff.
We may want other variables to represent other ideas, and I am not opposed to more variables, but we should clarify the existing ones and stick to our definitions of them.

There is a divergence between jit schema syntax and codegen native_functions parsing syntax:
In torch/csrc/jit/frontend/function_schema_parser.cpp, to specify that a list is aliased, you write T[](a), but this syntax is not supported in codegen. Likewise, Tensor(a)[] is not supported by jit's schema parser - edit: technically it is, but the end result is that the alias_info is nullopt.
This means that for functions like chunk, split, unbind, etc. that are currently defined with a signature having return of Tensor(a)[], their op.schema().returns()[0].alias_info().has_value() is false.
nodes.title: native_functions.yaml schema and jit schema divergence for aliased list
